title: The Fundamental Memory Ceiling of Noisy Quantum Reservoirs
authors: Markus Baumann, Jonas Stein, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien
abstract: Fresh qubits, not size, set how long a noisy quantum system can remember. With $k$ input qubits reinitialized per time step, the longest memory any reservoir can attain under depolarizing noise is $\exp[Θ(k)]$ time steps, whatever its size, dynamics, and input encoding. A universal upper bound and an explicit reservoir that attains the exponential scaling establish this optimal resource law. The bound depends on the dynamics only through the entropy that fresh qubits remove per time step, so it holds for any Markovian noisy dynamics without feedback, including measurement-free error correction.
summary: This work establishes a fundamental, exponential memory ceiling for noisy quantum reservoirs, proving that the memory retention time is dictated by the rate of fresh input qubits ($k$), not the physical size ($n$) of the system. The authors provide both an upper bound and an explicit construction that achieves this optimal scaling. This result sets a critical resource law for quantum information processing under realistic noise conditions.
main_problem: The paper determines the fundamental theoretical limit on how long a quantum system (reservoir) can retain memory when subjected to continuous depolarizing noise.
main_result: The memory depth is fundamentally limited by the rate at which fresh input qubits ($k$) are reinitialized, scaling exponentially as $\exp[O(k)]$, independent of the total reservoir size ($n$).
method: The proof analyzes the decay of distinguishability between two echo states corresponding to different input histories, utilizing entropy budgeting and purity constraints imposed by the noise channel.
model_or_system: The model is Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) using $n$ interacting qubits subjected to depolarizing noise at every time step. Information is injected via $k$ reinitialized input qubits.
key_observables: Memory Depth ($W(\epsilon)$), Purity ($\log_2 P_2$), Trace Distance between echo states.
important_parameters: Number of fresh input qubits ($k$), Reservoir size ($n$), Noise parameter ($q$), Error tolerance ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes Markovian dynamics without classical feedback, and the bound applies to any unital noise channel.
figures_summary: Figures schematically demonstrate that both the theoretical upper bound and an achievable lower bound scale exponentially with $k$, confirming the resource law.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by defining the noisy QRC setup, derives the exponential upper bound using entropy arguments, and then constructs an explicit error-correcting reservoir that achieves this lower bound, contrasting it with standard reservoir behavior.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, fundamental resource law for quantum memory storage, showing that the input rate ($k$) is the bottleneck, which is crucial for designing robust quantum computation protocols.

figures.caption: FIG. 2. Noisy quantum reservoir computing. (a) Forecasting yt+1 = 0.7 ut +0.3 ut−100 needs a memory of 100 time steps. (b) Every time step reinitializes k input qubits in σ(ut), applies a fixed unitary U to all n qubits, and depolarizes every qubit; a linear readout predicts ˆyt+1. Noise injects entropy into all n qubits, but only the k input qubits carry it out.

FIG. 3. The memory limit (schematic). (a) The optimum over reservoir sizes lies between two exponentials in k (Theorem 1); A, B, and C mark the reservoirs of (b). (b) One input stream drives three reservoirs: A and B differ tenfold in size but share k = 2 input qubits, and C is A with two more input qubits. Inputs older than the bound (red) are out of reach for every reservoir with the same k, so A and B share the bound Wq,2, and C’s bound Wq,4 lies further back.

FIG. 4. Attaining the limit. (a) Error-correcting reservoir (r = 3, k = 5): U writes the new bit, or the majority of the stored copies, into fresh ancillas and swaps them into the memory; the old copies leave with the input register. (b) With its fresh qubits used for repair, the memory depth of the error-correcting reservoir (exact single-qubit readout, n = 2k −2) grows exponentially with k, above the lower bound of Theorem 1; without repair (gray), the same r = k−2 copies gain almost nothing.
